# Generalized hydrodynamics: an interacting fluid of quasiparticles {#sec-ghd}

Join two integrable gases prepared at different temperatures or densities.
Particles collide repeatedly, yet the ensuing profiles often expand over a
region proportional to time rather than to its square root. Ordinary diffusion
has discarded the stable excitations responsible for this motion. Generalized
hydrodynamics, abbreviated GHD, retains their entire local rapidity distribution.

The essential prerequisite is a thermodynamic description of quasiparticles.
We reconstruct it below so that the dynamical derivation can be followed
independently. Units are $\hbar=k_B=1$; lattice spin conventions elsewhere are
$S^a=\sigma^a/2$. An *Euler-scale* limit sends distances and times to infinity
with their ratio fixed. It keeps ballistic motion and discards gradient
corrections that are relatively smaller in that limit.

## The local state is a distribution

In the repulsive Lieb–Liniger model, a particle is labeled by rapidity $k$,
with bare momentum $p(k)=k$ and energy $e(k)=k^2$ in mass units $m=1/2$.
Let $\rho_p(k;x,t)dk$ count occupied rapidities per physical length, and let
$\rho_s=\rho_p+\rho_h$ count all allowed rapidity states. The filling
$\vartheta=\rho_p/\rho_s$ lies between zero and one. Its fermionic-looking
range describes Bethe quantum numbers, not the exchange statistics of the atoms.

The local density-of-states relation is

$$
2\pi\rho_s(k)=p'(k)+\int dq\,K(k-q)\rho_p(q),
\qquad K(q)=\frac{2c}{c^2+q^2},\quad c>0.
$$ {#eq-ghd-state}

The interaction strength is $c$. The kernel is a derivative of the two-body
scattering phase. All quantities in @eq-ghd-state are evaluated in the same
local cell $(x,t)$. The equation follows by differentiating Bethe quantization;
@sec-integrability develops that construction.

For each conserved charge $Q[h]$, a particle carries a bare eigenvalue $h(k)$.
Its local density is $q[h]=\int dk\,\rho_p h$. Particle number uses $h=1$,
momentum $h=k$, and energy $h=k^2$. Knowing only these three moments does not
specify the function $\rho_p$. A local generalized Gibbs ensemble supplies the
larger family of constraints.

The hydrodynamic assumption is that a cell has relaxed sufficiently to such a
stationary macrostate before its parameters change appreciably. Coherent
microscopic oscillations, very sharp fronts, and special low-entropy preparations
can require additional variables or quantum corrections. GHD is not a
replacement for the exact wavefunction on every scale.

## Derivation of the effective velocity

A particle moving through a medium experiences scattering delays. Its
trajectory speed differs from its isolated group velocity
$v^{\mathrm{bare}}=e'/p'$. Since collisions preserve rapidities in an integrable
model, these delays can be accumulated without introducing a collision term that
changes the population of rapidities.

A compact way to sum the background response is *dressing*. For any bare
function $h(k)$, solve

$$
h^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)=h(k)+\int\frac{dq}{2\pi}
K(k-q)\vartheta(q)h^{\mathrm{dr}}(q).
$$ {#eq-ghd-dressing}

The density equation implies $(p')^{\mathrm{dr}}=2\pi\rho_s$.
Adding a quasiparticle shifts the momenta and energies of surrounding particles;
the ratio of the resulting energy and momentum derivatives is

$$
v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)=\frac{(e')^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)}{(p')^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)}.
$$ {#eq-ghd-effective-velocity}

This ratio can be turned into a kinetic equation. Multiply both sides by
$(p')^{\mathrm{dr}}$, use dressing of $e'$, and replace
$\vartheta(p')^{\mathrm{dr}}/(2\pi)$ by $\rho_p$. The result is

$$
v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)=v^{\mathrm{bare}}(k)+\frac1{p'(k)}
\int dq\,K(k-q)\rho_p(q)
[v^{\mathrm{eff}}(q)-v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)].
$$ {#eq-ghd-kinetic-velocity}

The relative velocity sets a collision rate; the scattering phase derivative
sets the signed displacement per encounter. For this convention, a sufficiently
fast Lieb–Liniger particle is slowed by encounters with slower particles. The
formula is self-consistent because collision partners are themselves dressed.
Replacing their velocities by bare ones is an additional approximation.

This derivation also explains how interactions can affect ballistic transport
without destroying it. Collisions change trajectories and observable currents,
but factorization prevents generic redistribution of the rapidity labels.
In models with several species, each density, kernel, and dressed quantity gains
a species index and the integrals include a species sum. Spin chains require
that extension, including their bound states.

## Conservation of quasiparticles and the GHD equation

A rapidity bin is conserved while its particles move with $v^{\mathrm{eff}}$.
The leading continuity equation is therefore

$$
\partial_t\rho_p(k;x,t)+\partial_x
\left[v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k;x,t)\rho_p(k;x,t)\right]=0.
$$ {#eq-ghd-euler}

Integrating against $h(k)$ gives conservation of every charge and its current:

$$
\partial_t q[h]+\partial_xj[h]=0,
\qquad
j[h]=\int dk\,\rho_p(k)v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)h(k).
$$ {#eq-ghd-charge-current}

The physical current is nonlinear in the local state even though it looks like
a sum of single-particle contributions: both the density of states and the
velocities depend on the full distribution. This is the predictive closure
missing from continuity alone. GHD was introduced independently by
@castro2016ghd and @bertini2016ghd.

An equivalent form reveals convenient state coordinates. From dressing,

$$
v^{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_s=
\frac{e'}{2\pi}+\int\frac{dq}{2\pi}
K(k-q)v^{\mathrm{eff}}(q)\rho_p(q).
$$

Differentiate the density-of-states equation in time and this identity in space.
For a homogeneous Hamiltonian, $p'$ and $e'$ have no space-time dependence;
@eq-ghd-euler then implies
$\partial_t\rho_s+\partial_x(v^{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_s)=0$.
Substitute $\rho_p=\vartheta\rho_s$ and cancel the latter continuity equation:

$$
\partial_t\vartheta(k;x,t)+v^{\mathrm{eff}}[\vartheta](k;x,t)
\partial_x\vartheta(k;x,t)=0.
$$ {#eq-ghd-filling-advection}

Thus the filling is constant along a characteristic satisfying
$dx/dt=v^{\mathrm{eff}}$. The characteristics interact through the state-dependent
speed. This is not independent free streaming, despite its advection form.

## Entropy at Euler order

The local Yang–Yang entropy per rapidity is
$s(k)=\rho_s(k)h(\vartheta(k))$, with
$h(v)=-v\ln v-(1-v)\ln(1-v)$.
Use filling advection and state-density continuity to obtain

$$
\partial_ts(k)+\partial_x[v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)s(k)]=0.
$$ {#eq-ghd-entropy}

After integration, thermodynamic entropy has a current but no local production
at Euler order. This does not forbid entanglement growth after a pure-state
quench. The coarse local entropy can already be nonzero after local relaxation,
and entanglement between regions changes as correlated quasiparticles cross
their boundaries. Euler transport of thermodynamic entropy and exact global
von Neumann entropy are distinct objects.

Diffusive corrections generally produce nonnegative entropy. Their appearance
is compatible with microscopic reversibility because coarse-graining discards
correlations among fluctuating trajectories.

## Solving a partitioning protocol

Prepare two homogeneous semi-infinite states with fillings
$\vartheta_L(k)$ and $\vartheta_R(k)$, then join them at $x=0$.
At late Euler times the solution depends on the ray $\zeta=x/t$.
Substituting into @eq-ghd-filling-advection gives

$$
[v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k;\zeta)-\zeta]\partial_\zeta\vartheta(k;\zeta)=0.
$$

Trace a characteristic backward: if its velocity exceeds the observation ray,
it reaches the left initial half; otherwise it reaches the right half. Hence

$$
\vartheta(k;\zeta)=
\begin{cases}
\vartheta_L(k),&v^{\mathrm{eff}}[\vartheta(\zeta)](k)>\zeta,\\
\vartheta_R(k),&v^{\mathrm{eff}}[\vartheta(\zeta)](k)<\zeta.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ghd-partitioning}

The equality set requires appropriate limiting treatment but normally has zero
measure for smooth observables. The selection is implicit: the selected
population changes the velocities used to select it. Iterative solution at
each ray alternates dressing with updating the left/right assignment.
One must check convergence rather than assuming every fixed-point iteration
is stable.

This protocol is called a *Riemann problem*: a conservation law starts from a
step between constant states. Unlike a simple fluid's finite list of sound and
contact modes, the integrable solution contains a continuum of characteristic
velocities, often with several bound-state families.

## Worked example: exact free-fermion domain-wall melting

Take a hopping chain
$H=-g\sum_x(c_x^\dagger c_{x+1}+c_{x+1}^\dagger c_x)$,
with $g>0$, dispersion $\epsilon(k)=-2g\cos k$, and velocity
$v(k)=2g\sin k$. Initially the left half is full and the right half empty.
The kernel vanishes, so no dressing is needed. At ray $\zeta$, occupied modes
are exactly those satisfying $2g\sin k>\zeta$.
For $|\zeta|<2g$, direct integration gives

$$
n(\zeta)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{dk}{2\pi}
\Theta(2g\sin k-\zeta)
=\frac1\pi\arccos\frac{\zeta}{2g},
$$ {#eq-ghd-free-density}

and

$$
j(\zeta)=\int\frac{dk}{2\pi}\,2g\sin k\,
\Theta(2g\sin k-\zeta)
=\frac{2g}{\pi}\sqrt{1-\frac{\zeta^2}{4g^2}}.
$$ {#eq-ghd-free-current}

Outside the cone, $n=1$ on the left and $n=0$ on the right, with zero current.
The central current is $2g/\pi$, and transferred particle number grows linearly
in time. Differentiating the two profiles checks
$-\zeta n'(\zeta)+j'(\zeta)=0$.
The calculation is exact in the Euler scaling limit. Microscopic fronts retain
lattice oscillations and narrower scaling regions not described by this formula.

A short Julia quadrature reproduces the profiles without evaluating a
many-body wavefunction:

```julia
#| eval: false
g = 1.0
Nk = 200000
k = (-pi .+ (0:Nk-1) .* (2pi/Nk))
v = 2g .* sin.(k)
for zeta in range(-1.8g, 1.8g, length=9)
    occ = v .> zeta
    density = sum(occ)/Nk
    current = sum(v .* occ)/Nk
    @show zeta density current acos(zeta/(2g))/pi
end
```

For a microscopic benchmark, evolve the correlation matrix
$C(t)=e^{-iht}C(0)e^{iht}$ of the one-particle hopping matrix $h$ and compare
$C_{xx}(t)$ at fixed $x/t$. Increase the chain length before increasing time
until boundaries no longer affect the chosen rays.

## Forces, diffusion, and breaking integrability

A smooth potential $V(x)$ coupling to particle number in the Lieb–Liniger gas
accelerates rapidities with $F=-\partial_xV$ in the stated units. Leading
hydrodynamics becomes

$$
\partial_t\rho_p+\partial_x(v^{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_p)
+\partial_k(F\rho_p)=0.
$$ {#eq-ghd-forced}

The potential must vary slowly on microscopic lengths. It breaks exact global
translation invariance, but a locally homogeneous scattering description may
remain accurate. More general couplings have dressed effective accelerations;
the simple $F$ above should not be transplanted indiscriminately.

At the next gradient order, quasiparticle trajectories fluctuate because the
number and rapidities of collision partners fluctuate. A schematic extension is

$$
\partial_t\rho_p+\partial_x(v^{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_p)
=\partial_x\!\left[\mathfrak D[\rho_p]\partial_x\rho_p\right]
+\mathcal I[\rho_p].
$$ {#eq-ghd-corrections}

The operator $\mathfrak D$ mixes rapidities and species; its normalization is
chosen here without an additional $1/2$. The collision integral $\mathcal I$
represents genuine rapidity-changing integrability breaking. Diffusion exists
even at exact integrability and must not be confused with $\mathcal I$.
@denardis2019diffusion derives diffusive transport using quasiparticle scattering
and form factors. At a symmetry point where the nominal diffusion coefficient
diverges, a different scaling treatment is required.

A weak perturbation often creates a long interval of GHD behavior before
ordinary hydrodynamics emerges. Relaxation-time models simplify $\mathcal I$
while preserving selected exact charges; @santra2026crossover explores this
route. Its usefulness depends on whether the true hierarchy of collision rates
is represented adequately.

## Correlation propagation and a numerical conservation test

Linearize GHD around a homogeneous stationary macrostate. To first order,
$\delta\vartheta(k;x,t)$ travels with the background velocity
$v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)$; the perturbation of the velocity multiplies a background
spatial derivative, which vanishes. The independent normal coordinates are thus
small filling fluctuations labeled by rapidity.
Thermodynamics assigns them occupation variance $\vartheta(1-\vartheta)$.
A charge perturbation couples through its dressed charge, because the surrounding
roots shift when a mode is added. Combining ballistic propagation with this
thermodynamic covariance gives the Euler two-point formula

$$
C_{ij}(x,t)\simeq\int dk\,\rho_p(k)[1-\vartheta(k)]
h_i^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)h_j^{\mathrm{dr}}(k)
\delta[x-v^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)t].
$$ {#eq-ghd-euler-correlations}

For multiple species, add their contributions with the appropriate model's
thermodynamic convention. The delta functions indicate ballistic rays at Euler
resolution; diffusion broadens them at finer resolution. Integrating over $x$
recovers the static charge covariance, providing a normalization check. Integrating
$x^2C$ explains ballistic second moments when the relevant charge has a nonzero
Euler projection. A particular observable can have a vanishing ballistic
projection by symmetry; its leading visible transport then comes from a
subleading or singular sector. Integrability does not force every charge to
show a nonzero ballistic signal in every state.

For actual computation, a conservation-form solver and a filling-advection
solver should approach the same smooth solution. A finite-volume method stores
cell-averaged $\rho_p$ and updates them with differences of interface fluxes.
The flux is recomputed from dressed velocities in each local state. Fluxes at
internal boundaries cancel exactly, so total discretized charges can be
monitored. An advection solver may be efficient but need not conserve those
integrals exactly on a finite grid. Neither scheme automatically preserves
$0\leq\vartheta\leq1$ without an appropriate interpolation or limiter.
The time step must resolve the fastest retained characteristic; rapidity
truncation can underestimate that speed and hide a stability problem.

![A Julia covariance-matrix calculation for a closed $L=240$ free-fermion chain
with hopping $g=1$ and a full/empty domain wall. Density profiles at $t=12,24,36$
collapse on ballistic rays; the current at $t=36$ agrees with the Euler curve.
Microscopic front rounding remains visible.](figs/ghd-domain-wall.png){#fig-ghd-domain-wall width=95%}

The reproducible calculation is in
[numerics/transport_labs.jl](numerics/transport_labs.jl). It checks covariance
Hermiticity, occupation bounds, total particle number, positive rightward current,
and agreement with the interior Euler profile at the specified times. These checks test this exactly
free benchmark. They do not validate a Bethe kernel or prove a general
interacting GHD solver correct.

## Research bridges and frontier questions

A productive first reproduction of @bertini2016ghd is the partitioning profile:
prepare the two thermal states, calculate their root densities, solve the
ray-dependent filling equation, and compare currents as well as densities to
TEBD. Matching one density profile can hide a normalization or missing-species
error; an independent current is a stronger check.

@alba2017entanglement supplies the related quasiparticle picture for entropy.
For homogeneous pair-producing quenches, the interval formula has the form
$S_\ell(t)=\sum_a\int dk\,s_a(k)\min(2|v_a^{\mathrm{eff}}(k)|t,\ell)$.
Each pair contributes only when one member is inside the interval and the other
outside. The factor two follows from opposite partners. Inhomogeneous states,
more complicated initial correlations, and other entropy measures can require
extensions; this is not a universal formula for arbitrary states.

The 2026 paper @scopa2026bloch extends forced GHD to finite-density impurities
in the Yang–Gaudin gas and predicts Bloch oscillations without a lattice, with
bound states changing the oscillation period. The broad perspective
@doyon2025perspective identifies a continuing challenge: combining Euler
transport with quantum fluctuations and correlations in preparations for which
local quasiparticle thermodynamics alone is insufficient.

## Exercises and selected solutions

1. Derive @eq-ghd-kinetic-velocity from dressing, keeping all factors of $2\pi$.
2. Show that the root-density equation and particle continuity imply state-density
   continuity, and then derive filling advection.
3. Derive both free-domain-wall profiles and verify the continuity equation on
   every interior ray.
4. Replace the full/empty halves by Fermi distributions with distinct temperatures
   and chemical potentials. Compute particle and energy currents at $\zeta=0$.
5. Show that the forced equation conserves total particle number and the total
   energy including $V(x)$, assuming no boundary flux.
6. Design a numerical comparison that distinguishes an Euler error from a
   rapidity-discretization error and a TEBD truncation error.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution: conservation in a smooth static potential"}
Integrating @eq-ghd-forced over $k$ and $x$ gives zero boundary terms, hence
constant particle number. For total energy
$E=\int dx\,dk\,[k^2+V(x)]\rho_p$, integration by parts gives
$\dot E=\int dx\,[V'j_n+Fj_p]$, where
$j_p=\int dk\,2k\rho_p$ and
$j_n=\int dk\,v^{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_p$.
For the Galilean Lieb–Liniger gas, $j_n=2\int dk\,k\rho_p=j_p$; the symmetry
of the scattering kernel makes collision shifts cancel in the total particle
current. Thus $F=-V'$ cancels the two terms. Establishing this current identity
is part of applying the model's Galilean symmetry consistently.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution sketch: the characteristic selection"}
For free particles, backward propagation from $(x,t)$ reaches initial point
$x_0=x-vt=t(\zeta-v)$. It is negative exactly when $v>\zeta$, producing the
left occupation in @eq-ghd-partitioning. In interacting GHD, the trajectory
speed depends on the local state, but the self-similar solution obeys the same
implicit left/right condition. Replacing $v^{\mathrm{eff}}$ by $v^{\mathrm{bare}}$
would ignore the medium and fail at finite interaction and density.
:::
